messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 58
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Dentist
  trauma_type: Police violence
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid All Feelings: avoid anything that could cause negative or positive feelings, Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
  Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
  Negative Appraisals: Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

David, at fifty-eight, had spent three decades building a life of meticulous order. His dental practice in the city suburbs was a testament to this, a place of quiet precision where every instrument had its place and every appointment ran on time. That order was shattered nine months ago on a rainy Tuesday evening. Driving home from a continuing education course, the sudden flash of blue and red lights in his rearview mirror was a surprise, but not an alarm. He pulled over calmly, expecting a ticket for a broken taillight. What followed was a blur of incomprehensible violence. Two officers, shouting commands he couldn't process fast enough, dragged him from his car. Before he understood what was happening, his cheek was pressed against the wet, gritty asphalt, the immense pressure of a knee grinding into his right shoulder blade. The world shrank to the smell of rain on pavement and the crackle of a police radio near his ear, spitting out clipped, urgent phrases. It was a case of mistaken identity, a suspect in a robbery who drove a similar car. They let him go twenty minutes later with a brusque apology, but the man who drove home was not the same one who had been pulled over.

In the weeks that followed, sleep became an impossibility. He would lie awake for hours, his body rigid, listening to every creak of the house. When exhaustion finally claimed him, he would be jolted awake by the disembodied sound of radio static, a phantom pain flaring sharply in his shoulder. The memories, when they came during the day, were strangely distant. He would see it unfold as if watching a film about a stranger, a grey-haired man in a nice suit being brutalized on the side of the road. It felt like it belonged to someone else, yet the pain in his shoulder was undeniably his own. He found himself constantly scanning his surroundings, a habit that began on the street but soon infiltrated every corner of his life. At restaurants with his partner, he could only sit in booths, his back pressed firmly against the wall, his eyes tracking every person who walked through the door. He felt a primal fear of strangers approaching him, a jolt of adrenaline whenever someone came up behind him in the grocery store aisle.

His work, once a source of pride, became a landscape of potential threats. The intimate space of the examination room felt suffocating. He was certain that there was something fundamentally wrong with him, some flaw in his character that had invited the attack. He would replay the traffic stop endlessly in his mind, convinced that if he had just moved slower, or spoken differently, it wouldn't have happened. This belief settled into a quiet, corrosive conviction that his life was irrevocably broken. The injustice of it all—that men could do this to him without consequence—was a constant, bitter presence. To manage the overwhelming feelings, David began to systematically dismantle his emotional world. He stopped listening to the classical music he once loved, finding its emotional swells unbearable. He and his partner had always enjoyed lively debates over dinner; now, he avoided any topic that could lead to stress or strong opinion. He was building a fortress of numbness, avoiding anything that could make him feel, whether good or bad. This bled into his practice. He started referring complex cases to colleagues, unable to bear the stress of a difficult procedure. The practice he had built with his own hands was now a place he endured.

The decision to seek therapy came after a moment of profound shame. A longtime patient, a friendly elderly woman, had reached back during a cleaning to pat his arm reassuringly, and he had flinched so violently he knocked a tray of instruments to the floor. The look of shock and concern on her face made him realize that the fortress he had built was becoming a prison, and he was losing not only himself but everything he had worked for. He came to his first session not with hope, but with the quiet desperation of a man who feels his world has been destroyed and is terrified that there is nothing left to salvage.
